chunks: Swapped PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage. The question: What happens if you swap the high-side PFET and the low-side NFET?
In a normal CMOS inverter the PMOS sits on top and the NMOS sits on the bottom. If you swap them, the circuit still conducts, but the output no longer reaches the rails.
Each transistor shuts itself off before the output gets all the way to its target. The circuit also stops inverting.
Picture climbing a ladder whose rungs vanish as you climb. Each step up removes a bit of your footing. You get most of the way and then there is nothing left to push against.
The swapped NMOS does this near the top. Its gate drive shrinks as its own source rises, so it stalls a threshold short of the supply.
Normal CMOS. Sources are at the rails, so the gate-source voltage of the active device is the full V DD and the output reaches the rails.
Source follower: a stage whose source copies the gate voltage minus a threshold. Threshold voltage ( V t ): the gate-to-source voltage needed to turn on.
Rail-to-rail: an output that swings all the way from ground to supply. Body effect: the threshold rising when the source is not at body voltage.
Non-inverting: the output follows the input instead of flipping it.
Use a 5 volts supply and give both transistors a 1 volts threshold ( V tn equals V tp equals 1 volts), with the NMOS now on top. Drive the input to 5 volts.
The output rises until it is about 5-1 equals 4 volts, and then the NMOS has no gate drive left and stops. Drive the input to 0 volts.
The PMOS at the bottom pulls the output down only to about 1 volts, one threshold above ground.
So the output swings from about 1 volts to 4 volts, and follows the input instead of flipping it. That is the whole idea.
"Swapping them puts the NMOS on top and the PMOS on the bottom, so each source is the output node.
The NMOS then can only pull the output up to V DD-V tn , since it turns off once its V GS falls to V t , and the PMOS can only pull it down to V tp .
So the output no longer reaches the rails, the body effect makes it worse, the edges get slower near the limits, and the stage becomes non-inverting.
That's why CMOS has the PMOS on top: its source sits at V DD so it gets full gate drive."
